This is a list of some of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=99 ōji Shrines}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the shrines in the region of 田辺市中辺路町. <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> [[Category:new pages]][[Category:new pages]][[Category:last 150 pages as of feb 11]][[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市中辺路町)]] ==Overview== == Kujūku Ōji of Tanabe City, Nakahechi (田辺市中辺路町の九十九王子) ==
[[Image:Takijiri-oji shrine 2.jpg|thumb|right|300px|One of the Goshintai Ōji, {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}]]
This article discusses the '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}''' located within the former {{ill|Nakahechi, Wakayama|ja|中辺路町}} area, now part of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}.
== What are the Kujūku Ōji? == {{Main|{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}}}
The '''Kujūku Ōji''' refers to a group of shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}}, especially along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路}} routes. They were rapidly organized during the 12th to 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners to serve as spiritual waypoints for imperial and noble pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}. Prayers for the protection of pilgrims were conducted at these shrines.
However, following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}} declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many Ōji along the Kiiji route. Despite efforts during the Edo period by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} to revitalize them, the shrines never fully regained their former prominence. The state-driven {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} policies of the Meiji era, shrine mergers, and urbanization further led to the loss or uncertainty of many shrine locations.
This article focuses on those Kujūku Ōji whose locations are identified within Tanabe City, specifically the former Nakahechi area.
== Monuments and Milestones == [[Image:Stupa of OSAKAMOTO-oji remains.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Stone stupa near {{ill|Osakamoto Ōji|ja|大阪本王子}}]]
Along the Nakahechi route, between {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}} and {{ill|Hongū Taisha|ja|本宮大社}}, distinct remnants can be observed:
One is the '''green schist monuments''' erected by the Kishū Domain in 1723 to commemorate the now-defunct Ōji sites.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 91]</ref> These can still be seen at places like Daimon, Hisohara, and Inohana.
Another is the '''stone stupas''' made of rhyolite, known as ''chōseki sotoba''.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 79]</ref> These served as distance markers, often engraved with Sanskrit characters, the distance from key points, and the names of donors.
== Sources == Key historical sources are abbreviated as follows:
{|class="wikitable" |+ Abbreviations of Historical Sources ! Abbreviation !! Author !! Year !! Notes |- ! 'Chūyūki' | {{ill|Fujiwara no Munetada|ja|藤原宗忠}} | 1109 | 'Chūyūki' |- ! 'Guki' | {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|ja|藤原定家}} | 1201 | Records of Kumano pilgrimage during Emperor Go-Toba’s reign. |}
== Kujūku Ōji of Nakahechi, Tanabe City == There are 13 Ōji shrines within this area, including {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}, {{ill|Daimon Ōji|ja|大門王子}}, {{ill|Chikatsuyu Ōji|ja|近露王子}}, and others, designated as part of the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja|熊野参詣道}}, a National Historic Site.<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2009-03-20}}</ref>

This article covers the shrines in the region of 田辺市中辺路町. <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> [[Category:new pages]][[Category:new pages]][[Category:last 150 pages as of feb 11]][[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市中辺路町)]] ==Overview== == Kujūku Ōji of Tanabe City, Nakahechi (田辺市中辺路町の九十九王子) ==
[[Image:Takijiri-oji shrine 2.jpg|thumb|right|300px|One of the Goshintai Ōji, {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}]]
This article discusses the '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}''' located within the former {{ill|Nakahechi, Wakayama|ja|中辺路町}} area, now part of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}.
== What are the Kujūku Ōji? == {{Main|{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}}}
The '''Kujūku Ōji''' refers to a group of shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}}, especially along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路}} routes. They were rapidly organized during the 12th to 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners to serve as spiritual waypoints for imperial and noble pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}. Prayers for the protection of pilgrims were conducted at these shrines.
However, following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}} declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many Ōji along the Kiiji route. Despite efforts during the Edo period by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} to revitalize them, the shrines never fully regained their former prominence. The state-driven {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} policies of the Meiji era, shrine mergers, and urbanization further led to the loss or uncertainty of many shrine locations.
This article focuses on those Kujūku Ōji whose locations are identified within Tanabe City, specifically the former Nakahechi area.
== Monuments and Milestones == [[Image:Stupa of OSAKAMOTO-oji remains.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Stone stupa near {{ill|Osakamoto Ōji|ja|大阪本王子}}]]
Along the Nakahechi route, between {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}} and {{ill|Hongū Taisha|ja|本宮大社}}, distinct remnants can be observed:
One is the '''green schist monuments''' erected by the Kishū Domain in 1723 to commemorate the now-defunct Ōji sites.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 91]</ref> These can still be seen at places like Daimon, Hisohara, and Inohana.
Another is the '''stone stupas''' made of rhyolite, known as ''chōseki sotoba''.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 79]</ref> These served as distance markers, often engraved with Sanskrit characters, the distance from key points, and the names of donors.

== Kujūku Ōji of Nakahechi, Tanabe City == There are 13 Ōji shrines within this area, including {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}, {{ill|Daimon Ōji|ja|大門王子}}, {{ill|Chikatsuyu Ōji|ja|近露王子}}, and others, designated as part of the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja|熊野参詣道}}, a National Historic Site.<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2009-03-20}}</ref>

This is a list of some of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=99 ōji Shrines}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the shrines in the region of 田辺市中辺路町. <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:last 150 pages as of feb 11]][[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市中辺路町)]] ==Overview== == Kujūku Ōji of Tanabe City, Nakahechi (田辺市中辺路町の九十九王子) ==
[[Image:Takijiri-oji shrine 2.jpg|thumb|right|300px|One of the Goshintai Ōji, {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}]]
This article discusses the '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}''' located within the former {{ill|Nakahechi, Wakayama|ja|中辺路町}} area, now part of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}.
== What are the Kujūku Ōji? == {{Main|{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}}}
The '''Kujūku Ōji''' refers to a group of shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}}, especially along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路}} routes. They were rapidly organized during the 12th to 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners to serve as spiritual waypoints for imperial and noble pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}. Prayers for the protection of pilgrims were conducted at these shrines.
However, following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}} declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many Ōji along the Kiiji route. Despite efforts during the Edo period by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} to revitalize them, the shrines never fully regained their former prominence. The state-driven {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} policies of the Meiji era, shrine mergers, and urbanization further led to the loss or uncertainty of many shrine locations.
This article focuses on those Kujūku Ōji whose locations are identified within Tanabe City, specifically the former Nakahechi area.
== Monuments and Milestones == [[Image:Stupa of OSAKAMOTO-oji remains.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Stone stupa near {{ill|Osakamoto Ōji|ja|大阪本王子}}]]
Along the Nakahechi route, between {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}} and {{ill|Hongū Taisha|ja|本宮大社}}, distinct remnants can be observed:
One is the '''green schist monuments''' erected by the Kishū Domain in 1723 to commemorate the now-defunct Ōji sites.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 91]</ref> These can still be seen at places like Daimon, Hisohara, and Inohana.
Another is the '''stone stupas''' made of rhyolite, known as ''chōseki sotoba''.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 79]</ref> These served as distance markers, often engraved with Sanskrit characters, the distance from key points, and the names of donors.
== Sources == Key historical sources are abbreviated as follows:
{|class="wikitable" |+ Abbreviations of Historical Sources ! Abbreviation !! Author !! Year !! Notes |- ! 'Chūyūki' | {{ill|Fujiwara no Munetada|ja|藤原宗忠}} | 1109 | 'Chūyūki' |- ! 'Guki' | {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|ja|藤原定家}} | 1201 | Records of Kumano pilgrimage during Emperor Go-Toba’s reign. |}
== Kujūku Ōji of Nakahechi, Tanabe City == There are 13 Ōji shrines within this area, including {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}, {{ill|Daimon Ōji|ja|大門王子}}, {{ill|Chikatsuyu Ōji|ja|近露王子}}, and others, designated as part of the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja|熊野参詣道}}, a National Historic Site.<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2009-03-20}}</ref>

This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:last 150 pages as of feb 11]][[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市中辺路町)]] ==Overview== == Kujūku Ōji of Tanabe City, Nakahechi (田辺市中辺路町の九十九王子) ==
[[Image:Takijiri-oji shrine 2.jpg|thumb|right|300px|One of the Goshintai Ōji, {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}]]
This article discusses the '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}''' located within the former {{ill|Nakahechi, Wakayama|ja|中辺路町}} area, now part of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}.
== What are the Kujūku Ōji? == {{Main|{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}}}
The '''Kujūku Ōji''' refers to a group of shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}}, especially along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路}} routes. They were rapidly organized during the 12th to 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners to serve as spiritual waypoints for imperial and noble pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}. Prayers for the protection of pilgrims were conducted at these shrines.
However, following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}} declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many Ōji along the Kiiji route. Despite efforts during the Edo period by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} to revitalize them, the shrines never fully regained their former prominence. The state-driven {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} policies of the Meiji era, shrine mergers, and urbanization further led to the loss or uncertainty of many shrine locations.
This article focuses on those Kujūku Ōji whose locations are identified within Tanabe City, specifically the former Nakahechi area.
== Monuments and Milestones == [[Image:Stupa of OSAKAMOTO-oji remains.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Stone stupa near {{ill|Osakamoto Ōji|ja|大阪本王子}}]]
Along the Nakahechi route, between {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}} and {{ill|Hongū Taisha|ja|本宮大社}}, distinct remnants can be observed:
One is the '''green schist monuments''' erected by the Kishū Domain in 1723 to commemorate the now-defunct Ōji sites.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 91]</ref> These can still be seen at places like Daimon, Hisohara, and Inohana.
Another is the '''stone stupas''' made of rhyolite, known as ''chōseki sotoba''.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 79]</ref> These served as distance markers, often engraved with Sanskrit characters, the distance from key points, and the names of donors.
== Sources == Key historical sources are abbreviated as follows:

== Kujūku Ōji of Nakahechi, Tanabe City == There are 13 Ōji shrines within this area, including {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}, {{ill|Daimon Ōji|ja|大門王子}}, {{ill|Chikatsuyu Ōji|ja|近露王子}}, and others, designated as part of the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja|熊野参詣道}}, a National Historic Site.<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2009-03-20}}</ref>

This article discusses the '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}''' located within the former {{ill|Nakahechi, Wakayama|ja|中辺路町}} area, now part of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}.
== What are the Kujūku Ōji? == {{Main|{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}}}
The '''Kujūku Ōji''' refers to a group of shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}}, especially along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路}} routes. They were rapidly organized during the 12th to 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners to serve as spiritual waypoints for imperial and noble pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}. Prayers for the protection of pilgrims were conducted at these shrines.
However, following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}} declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many Ōji along the Kiiji route. Despite efforts during the Edo period by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} to revitalize them, the shrines never fully regained their former prominence. The state-driven {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} policies of the Meiji era, shrine mergers, and urbanization further led to the loss or uncertainty of many shrine locations.
This article focuses on those Kujūku Ōji whose locations are identified within Tanabe City, specifically the former Nakahechi area.
== Monuments and Milestones == [[Image:Stupa of OSAKAMOTO-oji remains.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Stone stupa near {{ill|Osakamoto Ōji|ja|大阪本王子}}]]
Along the Nakahechi route, between {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}} and {{ill|Hongū Taisha|ja|本宮大社}}, distinct remnants can be observed:
One is the '''green schist monuments''' erected by the Kishū Domain in 1723 to commemorate the now-defunct Ōji sites.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 91]</ref> These can still be seen at places like Daimon, Hisohara, and Inohana.
Another is the '''stone stupas''' made of rhyolite, known as ''chōseki sotoba''.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 79]</ref> These served as distance markers, often engraved with Sanskrit characters, the distance from key points, and the names of donors.

This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:last 150 pages as of feb 11]][[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市中辺路町)]] ==Overview== == Kujūku Ōji of Tanabe City, Nakahechi (田辺市中辺路町の九十九王子) ==
[[Image:Takijiri-oji shrine 2.jpg|thumb|right|300px|One of the Goshintai Ōji, {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}]]
This article discusses the '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}''' located within the former {{ill|Nakahechi, Wakayama|ja|中辺路町}} area, now part of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}.
== What are the Kujūku Ōji? == {{Main|{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}}}
The '''Kujūku Ōji''' refers to a group of shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}}, especially along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路}} routes. They were rapidly organized during the 12th to 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners to serve as spiritual waypoints for imperial and noble pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}. Prayers for the protection of pilgrims were conducted at these shrines.
However, following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}} declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many Ōji along the Kiiji route. Despite efforts during the Edo period by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} to revitalize them, the shrines never fully regained their former prominence. The state-driven {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} policies of the Meiji era, shrine mergers, and urbanization further led to the loss or uncertainty of many shrine locations.
This article focuses on those Kujūku Ōji whose locations are identified within Tanabe City, specifically the former Nakahechi area.
== Monuments and Milestones == [[Image:Stupa of OSAKAMOTO-oji remains.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Stone stupa near {{ill|Osakamoto Ōji|ja|大阪本王子}}]]
Along the Nakahechi route, between {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}} and {{ill|Hongū Taisha|ja|本宮大社}}, distinct remnants can be observed:
One is the '''green schist monuments''' erected by the Kishū Domain in 1723 to commemorate the now-defunct Ōji sites.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 91]</ref> These can still be seen at places like Daimon, Hisohara, and Inohana.
Another is the '''stone stupas''' made of rhyolite, known as ''chōseki sotoba''.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 79]</ref> These served as distance markers, often engraved with Sanskrit characters, the distance from key points, and the names of donors.

== Kujūku Ōji of Nakahechi, Tanabe City == There are 13 Ōji shrines within this area, including {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}, {{ill|Daimon Ōji|ja|大門王子}}, {{ill|Chikatsuyu Ōji|ja|近露王子}}, and others, designated as part of the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja|熊野参詣道}}, a National Historic Site.<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2009-03-20}}</ref>

This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:last 150 pages as of feb 11]][[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市中辺路町)]] ==Overview== == Kujūku Ōji of Tanabe City, Nakahechi (田辺市中辺路町の九十九王子) ==
[[Image:Takijiri-oji shrine 2.jpg|thumb|right|300px|One of the Goshintai Ōji, {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}]]
This article discusses the '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}''' located within the former {{ill|Nakahechi, Wakayama|ja|中辺路町}} area, now part of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}.
== What are the Kujūku Ōji? == {{Main|{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}}}
The '''Kujūku Ōji''' refers to a group of shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}}, especially along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路}} routes. They were rapidly organized during the 12th to 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners to serve as spiritual waypoints for imperial and noble pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}. Prayers for the protection of pilgrims were conducted at these shrines.
However, following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}} declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many Ōji along the Kiiji route. Despite efforts during the Edo period by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} to revitalize them, the shrines never fully regained their former prominence. The state-driven {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} policies of the Meiji era, shrine mergers, and urbanization further led to the loss or uncertainty of many shrine locations.
This article focuses on those Kujūku Ōji whose locations are identified within Tanabe City, specifically the former Nakahechi area.
== Monuments and Milestones == [[Image:Stupa of OSAKAMOTO-oji remains.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Stone stupa near {{ill|Osakamoto Ōji|ja|大阪本王子}}]]
Along the Nakahechi route, between {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}} and {{ill|Hongū Taisha|ja|本宮大社}}, distinct remnants can be observed:
One is the '''green schist monuments''' erected by the Kishū Domain in 1723 to commemorate the now-defunct Ōji sites.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 91]</ref> These can still be seen at places like Daimon, Hisohara, and Inohana.
Another is the '''stone stupas''' made of rhyolite, known as ''chōseki sotoba''.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 79]</ref> These served as distance markers, often engraved with Sanskrit characters, the distance from key points, and the names of donors.

== Kujūku Ōji of Nakahechi, Tanabe City == There are 13 Ōji shrines within this area, including {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}, {{ill|Daimon Ōji|ja|大門王子}}, {{ill|Chikatsuyu Ōji|ja|近露王子}}, and others, designated as part of the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja|熊野参詣道}}, a National Historic Site.<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2009-03-20}}</ref>

This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:last 150 pages as of feb 11]][[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市中辺路町)]] ==Overview== == Kujūku Ōji of Tanabe City, Nakahechi (田辺市中辺路町の九十九王子) ==
[[Image:Takijiri-oji shrine 2.jpg|thumb|right|300px|One of the Goshintai Ōji, {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}]]
This article discusses the '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}''' located within the former {{ill|Nakahechi, Wakayama|ja|中辺路町}} area, now part of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}.
== What are the Kujūku Ōji? == {{Main|{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}}}
The '''Kujūku Ōji''' refers to a group of shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}}, especially along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路}} routes. They were rapidly organized during the 12th to 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners to serve as spiritual waypoints for imperial and noble pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}. Prayers for the protection of pilgrims were conducted at these shrines.
However, following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}} declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many Ōji along the Kiiji route. Despite efforts during the Edo period by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} to revitalize them, the shrines never fully regained their former prominence. The state-driven {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} policies of the Meiji era, shrine mergers, and urbanization further led to the loss or uncertainty of many shrine locations.
This article focuses on those Kujūku Ōji whose locations are identified within Tanabe City, specifically the former Nakahechi area.
== Monuments and Milestones == [[Image:Stupa of OSAKAMOTO-oji remains.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Stone stupa near {{ill|Osakamoto Ōji|ja|大阪本王子}}]]
Along the Nakahechi route, between {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}} and {{ill|Hongū Taisha|ja|本宮大社}}, distinct remnants can be observed:
One is the '''green schist monuments''' erected by the Kishū Domain in 1723 to commemorate the now-defunct Ōji sites.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 91]</ref> These can still be seen at places like Daimon, Hisohara, and Inohana.
Another is the '''stone stupas''' made of rhyolite, known as ''chōseki sotoba''.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 79]</ref> These served as distance markers, often engraved with Sanskrit characters, the distance from key points, and the names of donors.

== Kujūku Ōji of Nakahechi, Tanabe City == There are 13 Ōji shrines within this area, including {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}, {{ill|Daimon Ōji|ja|大門王子}}, {{ill|Chikatsuyu Ōji|ja|近露王子}}, and others, designated as part of the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja|熊野参詣道}}, a National Historic Site.<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2009-03-20}}</ref>

This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:last 150 pages as of feb 11]][[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市中辺路町)]] ==Overview== == Kujūku Ōji of Tanabe City, Nakahechi (田辺市中辺路町の九十九王子) ==
[[Image:Takijiri-oji shrine 2.jpg|thumb|right|300px|One of the Goshintai Ōji, {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}]]
This article discusses the '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}''' located within the former {{ill|Nakahechi, Wakayama|ja|中辺路町}} area, now part of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}.
== What are the Kujūku Ōji? == {{Main|{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}}}
The '''Kujūku Ōji''' refers to a group of shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}}, especially along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路}} routes. They were rapidly organized during the 12th to 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners to serve as spiritual waypoints for imperial and noble pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}. Prayers for the protection of pilgrims were conducted at these shrines.
However, following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}} declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many Ōji along the Kiiji route. Despite efforts during the Edo period by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} to revitalize them, the shrines never fully regained their former prominence. The state-driven {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} policies of the Meiji era, shrine mergers, and urbanization further led to the loss or uncertainty of many shrine locations.
This article focuses on those Kujūku Ōji whose locations are identified within Tanabe City, specifically the former Nakahechi area.
== Monuments and Milestones == [[Image:Stupa of OSAKAMOTO-oji remains.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Stone stupa near {{ill|Osakamoto Ōji|ja|大阪本王子}}]]
Along the Nakahechi route, between {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}} and {{ill|Hongū Taisha|ja|本宮大社}}, distinct remnants can be observed:
One is the '''green schist monuments''' erected by the Kishū Domain in 1723 to commemorate the now-defunct Ōji sites.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 91]</ref> These can still be seen at places like Daimon, Hisohara, and Inohana.
Another is the '''stone stupas''' made of rhyolite, known as ''chōseki sotoba''.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 79]</ref> These served as distance markers, often engraved with Sanskrit characters, the distance from key points, and the names of donors.

== Kujūku Ōji of Nakahechi, Tanabe City == There are 13 Ōji shrines within this area, including {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}, {{ill|Daimon Ōji|ja|大門王子}}, {{ill|Chikatsuyu Ōji|ja|近露王子}}, and others, designated as part of the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja|熊野参詣道}}, a National Historic Site.<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2009-03-20}}</ref>

This article discusses the '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}''' located within the former {{ill|Nakahechi, Wakayama|ja|中辺路町}} area, now part of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}.
== What are the Kujūku Ōji? == {{Main|{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}}}
The '''Kujūku Ōji''' refers to a group of shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}}, especially along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路}} routes. They were rapidly organized during the 12th to 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners to serve as spiritual waypoints for imperial and noble pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}. Prayers for the protection of pilgrims were conducted at these shrines.
However, following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}} declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many Ōji along the Kiiji route. Despite efforts during the Edo period by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} to revitalize them, the shrines never fully regained their former prominence. The state-driven {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} policies of the Meiji era, shrine mergers, and urbanization further led to the loss or uncertainty of many shrine locations.
This article focuses on those Kujūku Ōji whose locations are identified within Tanabe City, specifically the former Nakahechi area.
== Monuments and Milestones == [[Image:Stupa of OSAKAMOTO-oji remains.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Stone stupa near {{ill|Osakamoto Ōji|ja|大阪本王子}}]]
Along the Nakahechi route, between {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}} and {{ill|Hongū Taisha|ja|本宮大社}}, distinct remnants can be observed:
One is the '''green schist monuments''' erected by the Kishū Domain in 1723 to commemorate the now-defunct Ōji sites.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 91]</ref> These can still be seen at places like Daimon, Hisohara, and Inohana.
Another is the '''stone stupas''' made of rhyolite, known as ''chōseki sotoba''.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 79]</ref> These served as distance markers, often engraved with Sanskrit characters, the distance from key points, and the names of donors.

[[Image:Takijiri-oji shrine 2.jpg|thumb|right|300px|One of the Goshintai Ōji, {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}]]
This article discusses the '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}''' located within the former {{ill|Nakahechi, Wakayama|ja|中辺路町}} area, now part of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}.
== What are the Kujūku Ōji? == {{Main|{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}}}
The '''Kujūku Ōji''' refers to a group of shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}}, especially along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路}} routes. They were rapidly organized during the 12th to 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners to serve as spiritual waypoints for imperial and noble pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}. Prayers for the protection of pilgrims were conducted at these shrines.
However, following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}} declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many Ōji along the Kiiji route. Despite efforts during the Edo period by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} to revitalize them, the shrines never fully regained their former prominence. The state-driven {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} policies of the Meiji era, shrine mergers, and urbanization further led to the loss or uncertainty of many shrine locations.
This article focuses on those Kujūku Ōji whose locations are identified within Tanabe City, specifically the former Nakahechi area.
== Monuments and Milestones == [[Image:Stupa of OSAKAMOTO-oji remains.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Stone stupa near {{ill|Osakamoto Ōji|ja|大阪本王子}}]]
Along the Nakahechi route, between {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}} and {{ill|Hongū Taisha|ja|本宮大社}}, distinct remnants can be observed:
One is the '''green schist monuments''' erected by the Kishū Domain in 1723 to commemorate the now-defunct Ōji sites.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 91]</ref> These can still be seen at places like Daimon, Hisohara, and Inohana.
Another is the '''stone stupas''' made of rhyolite, known as ''chōseki sotoba''.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 79]</ref> These served as distance markers, often engraved with Sanskrit characters, the distance from key points, and the names of donors.

== Kujūku Ōji of Nakahechi, Tanabe City == There are 13 Ōji shrines within this area, including {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}, {{ill|Daimon Ōji|ja|大門王子}}, {{ill|Chikatsuyu Ōji|ja|近露王子}}, and others, designated as part of the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja|熊野参詣道}}, a National Historic Site.<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2009-03-20}}</ref>

This is a list of some of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=99 ōji Shrines}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the shrines in the region of 田辺市中辺路町. <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:Unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:qq-List of Kujūku Ōji (田辺市中辺路町)-qq]] [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:Unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:qq-List of Kujūku Ōji (田辺市中辺路町)-qq]] [[Category:last 150 pages as of feb 11]][[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市中辺路町)]] ==Overview== == Kujūku Ōji of Tanabe City, Nakahechi (田辺市中辺路町の九十九王子) ==
[[Image:Takijiri-oji shrine 2.jpg|thumb|right|300px|One of the Goshintai Ōji, {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}]]
This article discusses the '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}''' located within the former {{ill|Nakahechi, Wakayama|ja|中辺路町}} area, now part of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}.
== What are the Kujūku Ōji? == {{Main|{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}}}
The '''Kujūku Ōji''' refers to a group of shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}}, especially along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路}} routes. They were rapidly organized during the 12th to 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners to serve as spiritual waypoints for imperial and noble pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}. Prayers for the protection of pilgrims were conducted at these shrines.
However, following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}} declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many Ōji along the Kiiji route. Despite efforts during the Edo period by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} to revitalize them, the shrines never fully regained their former prominence. The state-driven {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} policies of the Meiji era, shrine mergers, and urbanization further led to the loss or uncertainty of many shrine locations.
This article focuses on those Kujūku Ōji whose locations are identified within Tanabe City, specifically the former Nakahechi area.
== Monuments and Milestones == [[Image:Stupa of OSAKAMOTO-oji remains.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Stone stupa near {{ill|Osakamoto Ōji|ja|大阪本王子}}]]
Along the Nakahechi route, between {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}} and {{ill|Hongū Taisha|ja|本宮大社}}, distinct remnants can be observed:
One is the '''green schist monuments''' erected by the Kishū Domain in 1723 to commemorate the now-defunct Ōji sites.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 91]</ref> These can still be seen at places like Daimon, Hisohara, and Inohana.
Another is the '''stone stupas''' made of rhyolite, known as ''chōseki sotoba''.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 79]</ref> These served as distance markers, often engraved with Sanskrit characters, the distance from key points, and the names of donors.
== Sources == Key historical sources are abbreviated as follows:
{|class="wikitable" |+ Abbreviations of Historical Sources ! Abbreviation !! Author !! Year !! Notes |- ! 'Chūyūki' | {{ill|Fujiwara no Munetada|ja|藤原宗忠}} | 1109 | 'Chūyūki' |- ! 'Guki' | {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|ja|藤原定家}} | 1201 | Records of Kumano pilgrimage during Emperor Go-Toba’s reign.|}
== Kujūku Ōji of Nakahechi, Tanabe City == There are 13 Ōji shrines within this area, including {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}, {{ill|Daimon Ōji|ja|大門王子}}, {{ill|Chikatsuyu Ōji|ja|近露王子}}, and others, designated as part of the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja|熊野参詣道}}, a National Historic Site.<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2009-03-20}}</ref>

This is a list of some of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=99 ōji Shrines}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the shrines in the region of 田辺市中辺路町. <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:Unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:qq-{{subst:MAINSPACE}}--qq]] [[Category:qq-List of Kujūku Ōji (田辺市中辺路町)-qq]] [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:Unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:qq-{{subst:MAINSPACE}}--qq]] [[Category:qq-List of Kujūku Ōji (田辺市中辺路町)-qq]] [[Category:last 150 pages as of feb 11]][[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市中辺路町)]] ==Overview== == Kujūku Ōji of Tanabe City, Nakahechi (田辺市中辺路町の九十九王子) ==
[[Image:Takijiri-oji shrine 2.jpg|thumb|right|300px|One of the Goshintai Ōji, {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}]]
This article discusses the '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}''' located within the former {{ill|Nakahechi, Wakayama|ja|中辺路町}} area, now part of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}.
== What are the Kujūku Ōji? == {{Main|{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}}}
The '''Kujūku Ōji''' refers to a group of shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}}, especially along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路}} routes. They were rapidly organized during the 12th to 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners to serve as spiritual waypoints for imperial and noble pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}. Prayers for the protection of pilgrims were conducted at these shrines.
However, following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}} declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many Ōji along the Kiiji route. Despite efforts during the Edo period by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} to revitalize them, the shrines never fully regained their former prominence. The state-driven {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} policies of the Meiji era, shrine mergers, and urbanization further led to the loss or uncertainty of many shrine locations.
This article focuses on those Kujūku Ōji whose locations are identified within Tanabe City, specifically the former Nakahechi area.
== Monuments and Milestones == [[Image:Stupa of OSAKAMOTO-oji remains.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Stone stupa near {{ill|Osakamoto Ōji|ja|大阪本王子}}]]
Along the Nakahechi route, between {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}} and {{ill|Hongū Taisha|ja|本宮大社}}, distinct remnants can be observed:
One is the '''green schist monuments''' erected by the Kishū Domain in 1723 to commemorate the now-defunct Ōji sites.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 91]</ref> These can still be seen at places like Daimon, Hisohara, and Inohana.
Another is the '''stone stupas''' made of rhyolite, known as ''chōseki sotoba''.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 79]</ref> These served as distance markers, often engraved with Sanskrit characters, the distance from key points, and the names of donors.
== Sources == Key historical sources are abbreviated as follows:
{|class="wikitable" |+ Abbreviations of Historical Sources ! Abbreviation !! Author !! Year !! Notes |- ! 'Chūyūki' | {{ill|Fujiwara no Munetada|ja|藤原宗忠}} | 1109 | 'Chūyūki' |- ! 'Guki' | {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|ja|藤原定家}} | 1201 | Records of Kumano pilgrimage during Emperor Go-Toba’s reign.|}
== Kujūku Ōji of Nakahechi, Tanabe City == There are 13 Ōji shrines within this area, including {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}, {{ill|Daimon Ōji|ja|大門王子}}, {{ill|Chikatsuyu Ōji|ja|近露王子}}, and others, designated as part of the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja|熊野参詣道}}, a National Historic Site.<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2009-03-20}}</ref>

This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:Unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:qq---qq]] [[Category:qq-List of Kujūku Ōji (田辺市中辺路町)-qq]] [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:Unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:qq---qq]] [[Category:qq-List of Kujūku Ōji (田辺市中辺路町)-qq]] [[Category:last 150 pages as of feb 11]][[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市中辺路町)]] ==Overview== == Kujūku Ōji of Tanabe City, Nakahechi (田辺市中辺路町の九十九王子) ==
[[Image:Takijiri-oji shrine 2.jpg|thumb|right|300px|One of the Goshintai Ōji, {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}]]
This article discusses the '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}''' located within the former {{ill|Nakahechi, Wakayama|ja|中辺路町}} area, now part of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}.
== What are the Kujūku Ōji? == {{Main|{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}}}
The '''Kujūku Ōji''' refers to a group of shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}}, especially along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路}} routes. They were rapidly organized during the 12th to 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners to serve as spiritual waypoints for imperial and noble pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}. Prayers for the protection of pilgrims were conducted at these shrines.
However, following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}} declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many Ōji along the Kiiji route. Despite efforts during the Edo period by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} to revitalize them, the shrines never fully regained their former prominence. The state-driven {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} policies of the Meiji era, shrine mergers, and urbanization further led to the loss or uncertainty of many shrine locations.
This article focuses on those Kujūku Ōji whose locations are identified within Tanabe City, specifically the former Nakahechi area.
== Monuments and Milestones == [[Image:Stupa of OSAKAMOTO-oji remains.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Stone stupa near {{ill|Osakamoto Ōji|ja|大阪本王子}}]]
Along the Nakahechi route, between {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}} and {{ill|Hongū Taisha|ja|本宮大社}}, distinct remnants can be observed:
One is the '''green schist monuments''' erected by the Kishū Domain in 1723 to commemorate the now-defunct Ōji sites.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 91]</ref> These can still be seen at places like Daimon, Hisohara, and Inohana.
Another is the '''stone stupas''' made of rhyolite, known as ''chōseki sotoba''.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 79]</ref> These served as distance markers, often engraved with Sanskrit characters, the distance from key points, and the names of donors.

== Kujūku Ōji of Nakahechi, Tanabe City == There are 13 Ōji shrines within this area, including {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}, {{ill|Daimon Ōji|ja|大門王子}}, {{ill|Chikatsuyu Ōji|ja|近露王子}}, and others, designated as part of the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja|熊野参詣道}}, a National Historic Site.<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2009-03-20}}</ref>

This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:Unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:qq---qq]] [[Category:qq-List of Kujūku Ōji (田辺市中辺路町)-qq]] [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:Unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:qq---qq]] [[Category:qq-List of Kujūku Ōji (田辺市中辺路町)-qq]] [[Category:last 150 pages as of feb 11]][[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市中辺路町)]] ==Overview== == Kujūku Ōji of Tanabe City, Nakahechi (田辺市中辺路町の九十九王子) ==
[[Image:Takijiri-oji shrine 2.jpg|thumb|right|300px|One of the Goshintai Ōji, {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}]]
This article discusses the '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}''' located within the former {{ill|Nakahechi, Wakayama|ja|中辺路町}} area, now part of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}.
== What are the Kujūku Ōji? == {{Main|{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}}}
The '''Kujūku Ōji''' refers to a group of shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}}, especially along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路}} routes. They were rapidly organized during the 12th to 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners to serve as spiritual waypoints for imperial and noble pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}. Prayers for the protection of pilgrims were conducted at these shrines.
However, following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}} declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many Ōji along the Kiiji route. Despite efforts during the Edo period by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} to revitalize them, the shrines never fully regained their former prominence. The state-driven {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} policies of the Meiji era, shrine mergers, and urbanization further led to the loss or uncertainty of many shrine locations.
This article focuses on those Kujūku Ōji whose locations are identified within Tanabe City, specifically the former Nakahechi area.
== Monuments and Milestones == [[Image:Stupa of OSAKAMOTO-oji remains.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Stone stupa near {{ill|Osakamoto Ōji|ja|大阪本王子}}]]
Along the Nakahechi route, between {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}} and {{ill|Hongū Taisha|ja|本宮大社}}, distinct remnants can be observed:
One is the '''green schist monuments''' erected by the Kishū Domain in 1723 to commemorate the now-defunct Ōji sites.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 91]</ref> These can still be seen at places like Daimon, Hisohara, and Inohana.
Another is the '''stone stupas''' made of rhyolite, known as ''chōseki sotoba''.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 79]</ref> These served as distance markers, often engraved with Sanskrit characters, the distance from key points, and the names of donors.

== Kujūku Ōji of Nakahechi, Tanabe City == There are 13 Ōji shrines within this area, including {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}, {{ill|Daimon Ōji|ja|大門王子}}, {{ill|Chikatsuyu Ōji|ja|近露王子}}, and others, designated as part of the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja|熊野参詣道}}, a National Historic Site.<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2009-03-20}}</ref>

[[Image:Takijiri-oji shrine 2.jpg|thumb|right|300px|One of the Goshintai Ōji, {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}]]
This article discusses the '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}''' located within the former {{ill|Nakahechi, Wakayama|ja|中辺路町}} area, now part of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}.
== What are the Kujūku Ōji? == {{Main|{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}}}
The '''Kujūku Ōji''' refers to a group of shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}}, especially along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路}} routes. They were rapidly organized during the 12th to 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners to serve as spiritual waypoints for imperial and noble pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}. Prayers for the protection of pilgrims were conducted at these shrines.
However, following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}} declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many Ōji along the Kiiji route. Despite efforts during the Edo period by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} to revitalize them, the shrines never fully regained their former prominence. The state-driven {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} policies of the Meiji era, shrine mergers, and urbanization further led to the loss or uncertainty of many shrine locations.
This article focuses on those Kujūku Ōji whose locations are identified within Tanabe City, specifically the former Nakahechi area.
== Monuments and Milestones == [[Image:Stupa of OSAKAMOTO-oji remains.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Stone stupa near {{ill|Osakamoto Ōji|ja|大阪本王子}}]]
Along the Nakahechi route, between {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}} and {{ill|Hongū Taisha|ja|本宮大社}}, distinct remnants can be observed:
One is the '''green schist monuments''' erected by the Kishū Domain in 1723 to commemorate the now-defunct Ōji sites.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 91]</ref> These can still be seen at places like Daimon, Hisohara, and Inohana.
Another is the '''stone stupas''' made of rhyolite, known as ''chōseki sotoba''.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 79]</ref> These served as distance markers, often engraved with Sanskrit characters, the distance from key points, and the names of donors.
== Sources == Key historical sources are abbreviated as follows:

== Kujūku Ōji of Nakahechi, Tanabe City == There are 13 Ōji shrines within this area, including {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}, {{ill|Daimon Ōji|ja|大門王子}}, {{ill|Chikatsuyu Ōji|ja|近露王子}}, and others, designated as part of the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja|熊野参詣道}}, a National Historic Site.<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2009-03-20}}</ref>

Another is the '''stone stupas''' made of rhyolite, known as ''chōseki sotoba''.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 79]</ref> These served as distance markers, often engraved with Sanskrit characters, the distance from key points, and the names of donors.

[[Image:Takijiri-oji shrine 2.jpg|thumb|right|300px|One of the Goshintai Ōji, {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}]]
This article discusses the '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}''' located within the former {{ill|Nakahechi, Wakayama|ja|中辺路町}} area, now part of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}.
== What are the Kujūku Ōji? == {{Main|{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}}}
The '''Kujūku Ōji''' refers to a group of shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}}, especially along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路}} routes. They were rapidly organized during the 12th to 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners to serve as spiritual waypoints for imperial and noble pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}. Prayers for the protection of pilgrims were conducted at these shrines.
However, following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}} declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many Ōji along the Kiiji route. Despite efforts during the Edo period by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} to revitalize them, the shrines never fully regained their former prominence. The state-driven {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} policies of the Meiji era, shrine mergers, and urbanization further led to the loss or uncertainty of many shrine locations.
This article focuses on those Kujūku Ōji whose locations are identified within Tanabe City, specifically the former Nakahechi area.
== Monuments and Milestones == [[Image:Stupa of OSAKAMOTO-oji remains.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Stone stupa near {{ill|Osakamoto Ōji|ja|大阪本王子}}]]
Along the Nakahechi route, between {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}} and {{ill|Hongū Taisha|ja|本宮大社}}, distinct remnants can be observed:
One is the '''green schist monuments''' erected by the Kishū Domain in 1723 to commemorate the now-defunct Ōji sites.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 91]</ref> These can still be seen at places like Daimon, Hisohara, and Inohana.
Another is the '''stone stupas''' made of rhyolite, known as ''chōseki sotoba''.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 79]</ref> These served as distance markers, often engraved with Sanskrit characters, the distance from key points, and the names of donors.

[[Image:Takijiri-oji shrine 2.jpg|thumb|right|300px|One of the Goshintai Ōji, {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}]]
This article discusses the '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}''' located within the former {{ill|Nakahechi, Wakayama|ja|中辺路町}} area, now part of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}.
== What are the Kujūku Ōji? == {{Main|{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}}}
The '''Kujūku Ōji''' refers to a group of shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}}, especially along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路}} routes. They were rapidly organized during the 12th to 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners to serve as spiritual waypoints for imperial and noble pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}. Prayers for the protection of pilgrims were conducted at these shrines.
However, following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}} declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many Ōji along the Kiiji route. Despite efforts during the Edo period by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} to revitalize them, the shrines never fully regained their former prominence. The state-driven {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} policies of the Meiji era, shrine mergers, and urbanization further led to the loss or uncertainty of many shrine locations.
This article focuses on those Kujūku Ōji whose locations are identified within Tanabe City, specifically the former Nakahechi area.
== Monuments and Milestones == [[Image:Stupa of OSAKAMOTO-oji remains.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Stone stupa near {{ill|Osakamoto Ōji|ja|大阪本王子}}]]
Along the Nakahechi route, between {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}} and {{ill|Hongū Taisha|ja|本宮大社}}, distinct remnants can be observed:
One is the '''green schist monuments''' erected by the Kishū Domain in 1723 to commemorate the now-defunct Ōji sites.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 91]</ref> These can still be seen at places like Daimon, Hisohara, and Inohana.
Another is the '''stone stupas''' made of rhyolite, known as ''chōseki sotoba''.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 79]</ref> These served as distance markers, often engraved with Sanskrit characters, the distance from key points, and the names of donors.

== Kujūku Ōji of Nakahechi, Tanabe City == There are 13 Ōji shrines within this area, including {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}, {{ill|Daimon Ōji|ja|大門王子}}, {{ill|Chikatsuyu Ōji|ja|近露王子}}, and others, designated as part of the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja|熊野参詣道}}, a National Historic Site.<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2009-03-20}}</ref>

[[Image:Takijiri-oji shrine 2.jpg|thumb|right|300px|One of the Goshintai Ōji, {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}]]
This article discusses the '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}''' located within the former {{ill|Nakahechi, Wakayama|ja|中辺路町}} area, now part of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}.
== What are the Kujūku Ōji? == {{Main|{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}}}
The '''Kujūku Ōji''' refers to a group of shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}}, especially along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路}} routes. They were rapidly organized during the 12th to 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners to serve as spiritual waypoints for imperial and noble pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}. Prayers for the protection of pilgrims were conducted at these shrines.
However, following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}} declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many Ōji along the Kiiji route. Despite efforts during the Edo period by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} to revitalize them, the shrines never fully regained their former prominence. The state-driven {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} policies of the Meiji era, shrine mergers, and urbanization further led to the loss or uncertainty of many shrine locations.
This article focuses on those Kujūku Ōji whose locations are identified within Tanabe City, specifically the former Nakahechi area.
== Monuments and Milestones == [[Image:Stupa of OSAKAMOTO-oji remains.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Stone stupa near {{ill|Osakamoto Ōji|ja|大阪本王子}}]]
Along the Nakahechi route, between {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}} and {{ill|Hongū Taisha|ja|本宮大社}}, distinct remnants can be observed:
One is the '''green schist monuments''' erected by the Kishū Domain in 1723 to commemorate the now-defunct Ōji sites.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 91]</ref> These can still be seen at places like Daimon, Hisohara, and Inohana.
Another is the '''stone stupas''' made of rhyolite, known as ''chōseki sotoba''.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 79]</ref> These served as distance markers, often engraved with Sanskrit characters, the distance from key points, and the names of donors.

== Kujūku Ōji of Nakahechi, Tanabe City == There are 13 Ōji shrines within this area, including {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}, {{ill|Daimon Ōji|ja|大門王子}}, {{ill|Chikatsuyu Ōji|ja|近露王子}}, and others, designated as part of the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja|熊野参詣道}}, a National Historic Site.<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2009-03-20}}</ref>

[[Image:Takijiri-oji shrine 2.jpg|thumb|right|300px|One of the Goshintai Ōji, {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}]]
This article discusses the '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}''' located within the former {{ill|Nakahechi, Wakayama|ja|中辺路町}} area, now part of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}.
== What are the Kujūku Ōji? == {{Main|{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}}}
The '''Kujūku Ōji''' refers to a group of shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}}, especially along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路}} routes. They were rapidly organized during the 12th to 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners to serve as spiritual waypoints for imperial and noble pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}. Prayers for the protection of pilgrims were conducted at these shrines.
However, following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}} declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many Ōji along the Kiiji route. Despite efforts during the Edo period by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} to revitalize them, the shrines never fully regained their former prominence. The state-driven {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} policies of the Meiji era, shrine mergers, and urbanization further led to the loss or uncertainty of many shrine locations.
This article focuses on those Kujūku Ōji whose locations are identified within Tanabe City, specifically the former Nakahechi area.
== Monuments and Milestones == [[Image:Stupa of OSAKAMOTO-oji remains.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Stone stupa near {{ill|Osakamoto Ōji|ja|大阪本王子}}]]
Along the Nakahechi route, between {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}} and {{ill|Hongū Taisha|ja|本宮大社}}, distinct remnants can be observed:
One is the '''green schist monuments''' erected by the Kishū Domain in 1723 to commemorate the now-defunct Ōji sites.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 91]</ref> These can still be seen at places like Daimon, Hisohara, and Inohana.
Another is the '''stone stupas''' made of rhyolite, known as ''chōseki sotoba''.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 79]</ref> These served as distance markers, often engraved with Sanskrit characters, the distance from key points, and the names of donors.

== Kujūku Ōji of Nakahechi, Tanabe City == There are 13 Ōji shrines within this area, including {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}, {{ill|Daimon Ōji|ja|大門王子}}, {{ill|Chikatsuyu Ōji|ja|近露王子}}, and others, designated as part of the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja|熊野参詣道}}, a National Historic Site.<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2009-03-20}}</ref>

[[Image:Takijiri-oji shrine 2.jpg|thumb|right|300px|One of the Goshintai Ōji, {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}]]
This article discusses the '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}''' located within the former {{ill|Nakahechi, Wakayama|ja|中辺路町}} area, now part of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}.
== What are the Kujūku Ōji? == {{Main|{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}}}}
The '''Kujūku Ōji''' refers to a group of shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}}, especially along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路}} routes. They were rapidly organized during the 12th to 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners to serve as spiritual waypoints for imperial and noble pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}. Prayers for the protection of pilgrims were conducted at these shrines.
However, following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}} declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many Ōji along the Kiiji route. Despite efforts during the Edo period by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} to revitalize them, the shrines never fully regained their former prominence. The state-driven {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} policies of the Meiji era, shrine mergers, and urbanization further led to the loss or uncertainty of many shrine locations.
This article focuses on those Kujūku Ōji whose locations are identified within Tanabe City, specifically the former Nakahechi area.
== Monuments and Milestones == [[Image:Stupa of OSAKAMOTO-oji remains.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Stone stupa near {{ill|Osakamoto Ōji|ja|大阪本王子}}]]
Along the Nakahechi route, between {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}} and {{ill|Hongū Taisha|ja|本宮大社}}, distinct remnants can be observed:
One is the '''green schist monuments''' erected by the Kishū Domain in 1723 to commemorate the now-defunct Ōji sites.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 91]</ref> These can still be seen at places like Daimon, Hisohara, and Inohana.
Another is the '''stone stupas''' made of rhyolite, known as ''chōseki sotoba''.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 79]</ref> These served as distance markers, often engraved with Sanskrit characters, the distance from key points, and the names of donors.

== Kujūku Ōji of Nakahechi, Tanabe City == There are 13 Ōji shrines within this area, including {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}, {{ill|Daimon Ōji|ja|大門王子}}, {{ill|Chikatsuyu Ōji|ja|近露王子}}, and others, designated as part of the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja|熊野参詣道}}, a National Historic Site.<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2009-03-20}}</ref>

This is a list of some of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=99 ōji Shrines}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the shrines in the region of 田辺市中辺路町. <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:Unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:qq---qq]] [[Category:qq-List of Kujūku Ōji (田辺市中辺路町)-qq]] [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:Unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:qq---qq]] [[Category:qq-List of Kujūku Ōji (田辺市中辺路町)-qq]] [[Category:last 150 pages as of feb 11]][[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市中辺路町)]] ==Overview== == Kujūku Ōji of Tanabe City, Nakahechi (田辺市中辺路町の九十九王子) ==
[[Image:Takijiri-oji shrine 2.jpg|thumb|right|300px|One of the Goshintai Ōji, {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}]]
This article discusses the '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji}}''' located within the former {{ill|Nakahechi, Wakayama|ja|中辺路町}} area, now part of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}.
== What are the Kujūku Ōji? == {{Main|{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji}}}}
The '''Kujūku Ōji''' refers to a group of shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道|1=Kumano Kodō}}, especially along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路|1=Kiiji}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路}} routes. They were rapidly organized during the 12th to 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners to serve as spiritual waypoints for imperial and noble pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}. Prayers for the protection of pilgrims were conducted at these shrines.
However, following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}} declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many Ōji along the Kiiji route. Despite efforts during the Edo period by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} to revitalize them, the shrines never fully regained their former prominence. The state-driven {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} policies of the Meiji era, shrine mergers, and urbanization further led to the loss or uncertainty of many shrine locations.
This article focuses on those Kujūku Ōji whose locations are identified within Tanabe City, specifically the former Nakahechi area.
== Monuments and Milestones == [[Image:Stupa of OSAKAMOTO-oji remains.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Stone stupa near {{ill|Osakamoto Ōji|ja|大阪本王子}}]]
Along the Nakahechi route, between {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}} and {{ill|Hongū Taisha|ja|本宮大社}}, distinct remnants can be observed:
One is the '''green schist monuments''' erected by the Kishū Domain in 1723 to commemorate the now-defunct Ōji sites.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 91]</ref> These can still be seen at places like Daimon, Hisohara, and Inohana.
Another is the '''stone stupas''' made of rhyolite, known as ''chōseki sotoba''.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 79]</ref> These served as distance markers, often engraved with Sanskrit characters, the distance from key points, and the names of donors.
== Sources == Key historical sources are abbreviated as follows:
{|class="wikitable" |+ Abbreviations of Historical Sources ! Abbreviation !! Author !! Year !! Notes |- ! 'Chūyūki' | {{ill|Fujiwara no Munetada|ja|藤原宗忠}} | 1109 | 'Chūyūki' |- ! 'Guki' | {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|ja|藤原定家}} | 1201 | Records of Kumano pilgrimage during Emperor Go-Toba’s reign.|}
== Kujūku Ōji of Nakahechi, Tanabe City == There are 13 Ōji shrines within this area, including {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}, {{ill|Daimon Ōji|ja|大門王子}}, {{ill|Chikatsuyu Ōji|ja|近露王子}}, and others, designated as part of the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja|熊野参詣道}}, a National Historic Site.<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2009-03-20}}</ref>

This is a list of some of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=99 ōji Shrines}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the shrines in the region of 田辺市中辺路町. <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:Unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:qq---qq]] [[Category:qq-List of Kujūku Ōji (田辺市中辺路町)-qq]] [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:Unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:qq---qq]] [[Category:qq-List of Kujūku Ōji (田辺市中辺路町)-qq]] [[Category:last 150 pages as of feb 11]][[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市中辺路町)]] ==Overview== == Kujūku Ōji of Tanabe City, Nakahechi (田辺市中辺路町の九十九王子) ==
[[Image:Takijiri-oji shrine 2.jpg|thumb|right|300px|One of the Goshintai Ōji, {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}]]
This article discusses the '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji}}''' located within the former {{ill|Nakahechi, Wakayama|ja|中辺路町}} area, now part of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}.
== What are the Kujūku Ōji? == {{Main|{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji}}}}
The '''Kujūku Ōji''' refers to a group of shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道|1=Kumano Kodō}}, especially along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路|1=Kiiji}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路}} routes. They were rapidly organized during the 12th to 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners to serve as spiritual waypoints for imperial and noble pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}. Prayers for the protection of pilgrims were conducted at these shrines.
However, following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}} declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many Ōji along the Kiiji route. Despite efforts during the Edo period by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} to revitalize them, the shrines never fully regained their former prominence. The state-driven {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} policies of the Meiji era, shrine mergers, and urbanization further led to the loss or uncertainty of many shrine locations.
This article focuses on those Kujūku Ōji whose locations are identified within Tanabe City, specifically the former Nakahechi area.
== Monuments and Milestones == [[Image:Stupa of OSAKAMOTO-oji remains.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Stone stupa near {{ill|Osakamoto Ōji|ja|大阪本王子}}]]
Along the Nakahechi route, between {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}} and {{ill|Hongū Taisha|ja|本宮大社}}, distinct remnants can be observed:
One is the '''green schist monuments''' erected by the Kishū Domain in 1723 to commemorate the now-defunct Ōji sites.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 91]</ref> These can still be seen at places like Daimon, Hisohara, and Inohana.
Another is the '''stone stupas''' made of rhyolite, known as ''chōseki sotoba''.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 79]</ref> These served as distance markers, often engraved with Sanskrit characters, the distance from key points, and the names of donors.
== Sources == Key historical sources are abbreviated as follows:
{|class="wikitable" |+ Abbreviations of Historical Sources ! Abbreviation !! Author !! Year !! Notes |- ! 'Chūyūki' | {{ill|Fujiwara no Munetada|ja|藤原宗忠}} | 1109 | 'Chūyūki' |- ! 'Guki' | {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|ja|藤原定家}} | 1201 | Records of Kumano pilgrimage during Emperor Go-Toba’s reign.|}
== Kujūku Ōji of Nakahechi, Tanabe City == There are 13 Ōji shrines within this area, including {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}, {{ill|Daimon Ōji|ja|大門王子}}, {{ill|Chikatsuyu Ōji|ja|近露王子}}, and others, designated as part of the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja|熊野参詣道}}, a National Historic Site.<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2009-03-20}}</ref>

This is a list of some of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=99 ōji Shrines}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the shrines in the region of 田辺市中辺路町. <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:Unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:qq---qq]] [[Category:qq-List of Kujūku Ōji (田辺市中辺路町)-qq]] [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ_Unlinked]][[Category:Unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:qq---qq]] [[Category:qq-List of Kujūku Ōji (田辺市中辺路町)-qq]] [[Category:last 150 pages as of feb 11]][[ja:九十九王子 (田辺市中辺路町)]] == Kujūku Ōji of Tanabe City, Nakahechi (田辺市中辺路町の九十九王子) ==
[[Image:Takijiri-oji shrine 2.jpg|thumb|right|300px|One of the Goshintai Ōji, {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}]]
This article discusses the '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji}}''' located within the former {{ill|Nakahechi, Wakayama|ja|中辺路町}} area, now part of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}.
== What are the Kujūku Ōji? == {{Main|{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji}}}}
The '''Kujūku Ōji''' refers to a group of shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道|1=Kumano Kodō}}, especially along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路|1=Kiiji}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路}} routes. They were rapidly organized during the 12th to 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners to serve as spiritual waypoints for imperial and noble pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}. Prayers for the protection of pilgrims were conducted at these shrines.
However, following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}} declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many Ōji along the Kiiji route. Despite efforts during the Edo period by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} to revitalize them, the shrines never fully regained their former prominence. The state-driven {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} policies of the Meiji era, shrine mergers, and urbanization further led to the loss or uncertainty of many shrine locations.
This article focuses on those Kujūku Ōji whose locations are identified within Tanabe City, specifically the former Nakahechi area.
== Monuments and Milestones == [[Image:Stupa of OSAKAMOTO-oji remains.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Stone stupa near {{ill|Osakamoto Ōji|ja|大阪本王子}}]]
Along the Nakahechi route, between {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}} and {{ill|Hongū Taisha|ja|本宮大社}}, distinct remnants can be observed:
One is the '''green schist monuments''' erected by the Kishū Domain in 1723 to commemorate the now-defunct Ōji sites.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 91]</ref> These can still be seen at places like Daimon, Hisohara, and Inohana.
Another is the '''stone stupas''' made of rhyolite, known as ''chōseki sotoba''.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 79]</ref> These served as distance markers, often engraved with Sanskrit characters, the distance from key points, and the names of donors.
== Sources == Key historical sources are abbreviated as follows:
{|class="wikitable" |+ Abbreviations of Historical Sources ! Abbreviation !! Author !! Year !! Notes |- ! 'Chūyūki' | {{ill|Fujiwara no Munetada|ja|藤原宗忠}} | 1109 | 'Chūyūki' |- ! 'Guki' | {{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|ja|藤原定家}} | 1201 | Records of Kumano pilgrimage during Emperor Go-Toba’s reign.|}
== Kujūku Ōji of Nakahechi, Tanabe City == There are 13 Ōji shrines within this area, including {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}}, {{ill|Daimon Ōji|ja|大門王子}}, {{ill|Chikatsuyu Ōji|ja|近露王子}}, and others, designated as part of the {{ill|Kumano Pilgrimage Route|ja|熊野参詣道}}, a National Historic Site.<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2009-03-20}}</ref>

This article discusses the '''{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji}}''' located within the former {{ill|Nakahechi, Wakayama|ja|中辺路町}} area, now part of {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|ja|田辺市}}.
== What are the Kujūku Ōji? == {{Main|{{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji}}}}
The '''Kujūku Ōji''' refers to a group of shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道|1=Kumano Kodō}}, especially along the {{ill|Kiiji|ja|紀伊路|1=Kiiji}} and {{ill|Nakahechi|ja|中辺路}} routes. They were rapidly organized during the 12th to 13th centuries by Kumano Shugendō practitioners to serve as spiritual waypoints for imperial and noble pilgrims on the {{ill|Kumano pilgrimage|ja|熊野詣}}. Prayers for the protection of pilgrims were conducted at these shrines.
However, following the {{ill|Jōkyū War|ja|承久の乱}} in 1221, pilgrimages from {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}} declined, leading to the deterioration and abandonment of many Ōji along the Kiiji route. Despite efforts during the Edo period by the {{ill|Kishū Domain|ja|紀州藩}} to revitalize them, the shrines never fully regained their former prominence. The state-driven {{ill|State Shinto|ja|国家神道}} policies of the Meiji era, shrine mergers, and urbanization further led to the loss or uncertainty of many shrine locations.
This article focuses on those Kujūku Ōji whose locations are identified within Tanabe City, specifically the former Nakahechi area.
== Monuments and Milestones == [[Image:Stupa of OSAKAMOTO-oji remains.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Stone stupa near {{ill|Osakamoto Ōji|ja|大阪本王子}}]]
Along the Nakahechi route, between {{ill|Takijiri Ōji|ja|滝尻王子}} and {{ill|Hongū Taisha|ja|本宮大社}}, distinct remnants can be observed:
One is the '''green schist monuments''' erected by the Kishū Domain in 1723 to commemorate the now-defunct Ōji sites.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 91]</ref> These can still be seen at places like Daimon, Hisohara, and Inohana.
Another is the '''stone stupas''' made of rhyolite, known as ''chōseki sotoba''.<ref>Kumanoji Editorial Committee [1973: 79]</ref> These served as distance markers, often engraved with Sanskrit characters, the distance from key points, and the names of donors.
